Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/README.md:64:#### Is it "npm" or "NPM" or "Npm"?
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/README.md:66:**`npm`** should never be capitalized unless it is being displayed in a location that is customarily all-capitals (ex. titles on `man` pages).
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/README.md:68:#### Is "npm" an acronym for "Node Package Manager"?
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/README.md:70:Contrary to popular belief, **`npm`** **is not** in fact an acronym for "Node Package Manager"; It is a recursive bacronymic abbreviation for **"npm is not an acronym"** (if the project was named "ninaa", then it would be an acronym). The precursor to **`npm`** was actually a bash utility named **"pm"**, which was the shortform name of **"pkgmakeinst"** - a bash function that installed various things on various platforms. If **`npm`** were to ever have been considered an acronym, it would be as "node pm" or, potentially "new pm".

Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/docs/content/using-npm/scripts.md:78:Since `npm@1.1.71`, the npm CLI has run the `prepublish` script for both `npm publish` and `npm install`, because it's a convenient way to prepare a package for use (some common use cases are described in the section below).  It has also turned out to be, in practice, [very confusing](https://github.com/npm/npm/issues/10074).  As of `npm@4.0.0`, a new event has been introduced, `prepare`, that preserves this existing behavior. A _new_ event, `prepublishOnly` has been added as a transitional strategy to allow users to avoid the confusing behavior of existing npm versions and only run on `npm publish` (for instance, running the tests one last time to ensure they're in good shape).

Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/docs/output/commands/npm.html:170:<p>You probably got npm because you want to install stuff.</p>

Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/docs/output/configuring-npm/folders.html:170:<p>Packages are dropped into the <code>node_modules</code> folder under the <code>prefix</code>.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/docs/output/configuring-npm/folders.html:174:<p>Global installs on Unix systems go to <code>{prefix}/lib/node_modules</code>.

As of <code>npm@4.0.0</code>, a new event has been introduced, <code>prepare</code>, that preserves this existing behavior. Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/man/man5/folders.5:12:Local install (default): puts stuff in \fB\|\./node_modules\fP of the current
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/man/man5/folders.5:15:Global install (with \fB\-g\fP): puts stuff in /usr/local or wherever node

Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/man/man5/folders.5:27:The \fBprefix\fP config defaults to the location where node is installed\.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/man/man5/folders.5:28:On most systems, this is \fB/usr/local\fP\|\. On Windows, it's \fB%AppData%\\npm\fP\|\.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/man/man5/folders.5:29:On Unix systems, it's one level up, since node is typically installed at
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/man/man5/folders.5:30:\fB{prefix}/bin/node\fP rather than \fB{prefix}/node\.exe\fP\|\.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/man/man5/folders.5:32:When the \fBglobal\fP flag is set, npm installs things into this prefix\.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/man/man5/folders.5:35:.SS Node Modules

Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:1:A handful of native addons require linking to OpenSSL in one way or another. This introduces a small challenge since node will sometimes bundle OpenSSL statically (the default for node >= v0.8.x), or sometimes dynamically link to the system OpenSSL (default for node <= v0.6.x).
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:8:    # node v0.6.x doesn't give us its build variables,
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:10:    # so default the variable to "true", v0.8.x node and up will overwrite it.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:11:    'node_shared_openssl%': 'true'
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:20:        ['node_shared_openssl=="false"', {
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:21:          # so when "node_shared_openssl" is "false", then OpenSSL has been
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:22:          # bundled into the node executable. So we need to include the same
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:23:          # header files that were used when building node.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:25:            '<(node_root_dir)/deps/openssl/openssl/include'
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:29:              "include_dirs": [ "<(node_root_dir)/deps/openssl/config/piii" ]
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:32:              "include_dirs": [ "<(node_root_dir)/deps/openssl/config/k8" ]
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:35:              "include_dirs": [ "<(node_root_dir)/deps/openssl/config/arm" ]
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:45:This ensures that when OpenSSL is statically linked into `node` then, the bundled OpenSSL headers are included, but when the system OpenSSL is in use, then only those headers will be used.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:49:As you can see this baseline `binding.gyp` file only accounts for the Unix scenario. Currently on Windows the situation is a little less ideal. On Windows, OpenSSL is _always_ statically compiled into the `node` executable, so ideally it would be possible to use that copy of OpenSSL when building native addons.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:51:Unfortunately it doesn't seem like that is possible at the moment, as there would need to be tweaks made to the generated `node.lib` file to include the openssl glue functions, or a new `openssl.lib` file would need to be created during the node build. I'm not sure which is the easiest/most feasible.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:53:In the meantime, one possible solution is using another copy of OpenSSL, which is what [`node-bcrypt`](https://github.com/ncb000gt/node.bcrypt.js) currently does. Adding something like this to your `binding.gyp` file's `"conditions"` block would enable this:
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:80:Now you can direct your users to install OpenSSL on Windows from here (be sure to tell them to install the 64-bit version if they're compiling against a 64-bit version of node): http://slproweb.com/products/Win32OpenSSL.html
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:82:Also note that both `node-gyp` and `npm` allow you to overwrite that default `openssl_root` variable on the command line:
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Linking-to-OpenSSL.md:85:$ node-gyp rebuild --openssl-root="C:\Users\Nathan\Desktop\openssl"

Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Updating-npm-bundled-node-gyp.md:9:Generally, npm's library files are installed inside your global "node_modules", where npm is installed (run `npm prefix` and add `lib/node_modules`, or just `node_modules` for Windows). There are some exceptions to this. Inside this global `node_modules/` there will be an `npm/` directory and inside this you'll find a `node_modules/node-gyp/` directory. So it may look something like `/usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/`. This is the version of node-gyp that ships with npm.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Updating-npm-bundled-node-gyp.md:11:When you install a _new_ version of node-gyp outside of npm, it'll go into your global node_modules, but not under the `npm/node_modules`. So that may look like `/usr/local/lib/node_modules/node-gyp/`. It'll have the `node-gyp` executable linked into your `PATH` so running `node-gyp` will use this version.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Updating-npm-bundled-node-gyp.md:13:The catch is that npm won't use this version unless you tell it to, it'll keep on using the one you have installed. You need to instruct it to by setting the `node_gyp` config variable (which goes into your `~/.npmrc`). You do this by running the `npm config set` command as below. Then npm will use the command in the path you supply whenever it needs to build a native addon.
Dependencies/npm.bundle/node_modules/npm/node_modules/node-gyp/docs/Updating-npm-bundled-node-gyp.md:15:**Important**: You also need to remember to unset this when you upgrade npm with a newer version of node-gyp, or you have to manually keep your globally installed node-gyp to date. See "Undo" below.
